statement: A symmetric (real) matrix M — Hermitian in the complex case — is positive semidefinite if x^T M x ≥ 0 for every real vector x (equivalently z*Mz ≥ 0 for every complex vector z). It is positive definite if the inequality is strict for every nonzero x. Writing M ≥ 0 denotes positive semidefiniteness; M ≥ N means M − N ≥ 0 (the Loewner order).

symbols.meaning: a second symmetric matrix, used for comparisons/ordering
test vector (real x,v; complex z) used in the quadratic-form condition

symbols.dimensions: n x n or n x m

properties.property: M ≥ N iff M − N is positive semidefinite; this defines a partial order (the Loewner order) on symmetric matrices, with a strict version M > N.
properties.why: definition of the induced ordering directly restates the PSD condition applied to a difference of matrices

properties.property: Every positive definite matrix is invertible and its inverse is also positive definite; if M ≥ N > 0 then N⁻¹ ≥ M⁻¹ > 0.
properties.why: inversion reverses the Loewner order for positive definite matrices

properties.property: If M, N are positive semidefinite, M + N is positive semidefinite; if M is positive definite and N positive semidefinite, M + N is positive definite.
properties.why: the defining quadratic form is additive: x^T(M+N)x = x^TMx + x^TNx, a sum of nonnegative terms

properties.property: If M is positive semidefinite, A*MA is positive semidefinite for any (possibly rectangular) A; if M is positive definite and A has full column rank, A*MA is positive definite.
properties.why: congruence transformation preserves the sign of the quadratic form: y*(A*MA)y = (Ay)*M(Ay)

properties.property: The diagonal entries m_ii of a PSD matrix are real and nonnegative, tr(M) ≥ 0, and |m_ij| ≤ √(m_ii·m_jj) for all i,j (so max_{i,j}|m_ij| ≤ max_i m_ii).
properties.why: every principal (in particular 2×2) submatrix of a PSD matrix is itself PSD, which forces these diagonal/off-diagonal bounds

properties.property: For any two PSD matrices M, N: tr(MN) ≥ 0.
properties.why: tr(MN) = tr(M^{1/2} N M^{1/2}), and M^{1/2}NM^{1/2} is PSD so its eigenvalues (and hence trace) are nonnegative

properties.property: If M, N ≥ 0, the Hadamard (entrywise) product M∘N ≥ 0, even though the ordinary product MN need not be PSD (Schur product theorem).
properties.why: stated as a distinct closure property of the PSD cone under the Hadamard product

properties.property: If M, N ≥ 0, the Kronecker product M⊗N ≥ 0, and the Frobenius inner product M:N ≥ 0.
properties.why: additional closure properties of the PSD cone under these products

properties.property: The set of PSD symmetric matrices is convex: if M, N are PSD, αM+(1−α)N is PSD for α∈[0,1].
properties.why: x^T(αM+(1−α)N)x = α·x^TMx + (1−α)·x^TNx ≥ 0, a convex combination of nonnegative terms; this convexity is what makes semidefinite programs converge to a global optimum

properties.property: For a block matrix M = [[A,B],[B*,D]] that is PSD, both diagonal blocks A and D must themselves be positive (semi)definite, and every principal submatrix of M is positive (semi)definite.
properties.why: testing z*Mz ≥ 0 on vectors z = [v,0]^T and z = [0,w]^T isolates v*Av ≥ 0 and w*Dw ≥ 0

properties.property: A Hermitian matrix is PSD iff all of its principal minors are nonnegative; checking only the leading principal minors is not sufficient (counterexample: diag(0, −1)).
properties.why: this is the standard minor-based test for semidefiniteness, with an explicit caveat distinguishing it from the (stronger) positive-definite leading-minor test

properties.property: A twice-differentiable function f has a local minimum at a critical point if its Hessian is PSD there; the quadratic form x^TMx itself has a unique minimum (zero) at x=0 exactly when M is positive definite.
properties.why: connects the algebraic PSD condition to second-order optimality conditions via the Hessian

properties.property: The covariance matrix of any multivariate probability distribution is always PSD (positive definite unless one variable is an exact linear function of the others); conversely every PSD matrix arises as the covariance matrix of some multivariate distribution.
properties.why: gives the canonical statistical example/characterization of PSD matrices

assumptions.assumption: The standard notion applies to symmetric (real) or Hermitian (complex) matrices M.
assumptions.breaks_when: M is non-symmetric/non-Hermitian: definiteness must then be assessed via the symmetric part ½(M+M^T) or Hermitian part ½(M+M*), since a non-symmetric M can have all-positive eigenvalues yet fail x^TMx>0 (e.g. M=[[4,9],[1,4]] with eigenvalues 1,7 gives x^TMx=−2 for x=[−1,1]^T).

failure_modes.mode: Concluding PSD from leading principal minors alone
failure_modes.signature: leading principal minors nonnegative but matrix is not PSD
failure_modes.cause: leading principal minors only certify positive definiteness of successive blocks; full PSD status requires all principal minors nonnegative (counterexample: diag(0,−1) has a nonnegative leading 1×1 minor but is not PSD)

failure_modes.mode: Using eigenvalue sign alone to judge PSD/definiteness of a non-symmetric matrix
failure_modes.signature: all eigenvalues positive/nonnegative yet x^TMx takes negative values for some x
failure_modes.cause: for non-symmetric M, eigenvalues do not determine the sign of the quadratic form; only the symmetric (Hermitian) part of M controls x^TMx
